name: River Gambia National Park
blurb: Baboon Islands: riverside forest, manatees, hippos and reintroduced chimps.

tip.title: Remove the chimpanzees
tip.text: Chimpanzees hunt red colobus and baboons. Select them and lower their numbers, then watch the monkeys that fed them and the trees those monkeys eat.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Raphia palm
nodes.desc: A palm of wet ground whose fruit is eaten by chimpanzees and baboons, and is a main food of palm-nut vultures.

nodes.name: Silk cotton tree
nodes.desc: A very tall forest tree. Its flowers and fruit are eaten by fruit bats.
A leaf-eating monkey of forest treetops. Wikipedia says common chimpanzees frequently hunt it.
Wikipedia says some hippos remain in the park, though they are now rare in the Gambia. They graze on land at night and rest in water by day.

nodes.name: Tilapia & other cichlids
nodes.desc: River fish that feed on plants and algae. They are the main prey for fish-eating birds and reptiles.
Hunts fish from a perch over open water, also takes waterbirds, and will eat carrion.
An unusual vulture that eats mostly oil palm and raphia fruit, with some fish, crabs, small animals and carrion.
A large water-loving lizard that hunts along the river and eats fish and other animals.
Wikipedia lists crocodiles among the reptiles of the park. Crocodiles take fish and are the main natural enemy of manatees in West Africa.

nodes.name: Common chimpanzee
nodes.desc: A reintroduced population lives on the Baboon Islands. Chimpanzees eat fruit and also hunt monkeys such as red colobus and Guinea baboons.
Tropical sun drives plant growth year round.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi, termites and bacteria that break down leaves, fallen fruit and dead animals.
